Act I

Scene i

[Enter Antonio and Delio.]

DELIO.

1You are welcome to your country, dear Antonio,
2You have been long in France, and you return
3A very formal Frenchman, in your habit.
4How do you like the French court?

ANTONIO.

How do you like the French court? I admire it;
5In seeking to reduce both State and people
6To a fixed order, their judicious King
7Begins at home. Quits first his royal palace
8Of flatt’ring sycophants, of dissolute,
9And infamous persons, which he sweetly terms
10His Master’s master-piece, the work of Heaven,
11Consid’ring duly, that a Prince’s court
12Is like a common fountain, whence should flow
13Pure silver-drops in general. But if’t chance
14Some cursed example poison’t near the head,
15Death and diseases through the whole land spread.
16And what is’t makes this blessed government,
17But a most provident Council, who dare freely
18Inform him, the corruption of the times?
19Though some o’th’court hold it presumption
20To instruct Princes what they ought to do,
21It is a noble duty to inform them
22What they ought to foresee. Here comes Bosola,
23[Enter Bosola] The only court-gall: yet I observe his railing
24Is not for simple love of piety:
25Indeed he rails at those things which he wants,
26Would be as lecherous, covetous, or proud,
27Bloody, or envious, as any man,
28If he had means to be so. Here’s the Cardinal.

[Enter Cardinal.]

BOSOLA.

I do haunt you still.

CARDINAL.

So.

BOSOLA.

I have done you better service than to be slighted thus.
Miserable age, where only the reward of doing well,
is the doing of it!

CARDINAL.

You enforce your merit too much.

BOSOLA.

I fell into the galleys in your service, where, for
two years together, I wore two towels instead of a shirt,
with a knot on the shoulder, after the fashion of a Roman
mantle. Slighted thus? I will thrive some way: blackbirds
fatten best in hard weather: why not I, in these dog days?

CARDINAL.

Would you could become honest,-

BOSOLA.

With all your divinity, do but direct me the way
to it. I have known many travel far for it, and yet return
as arrant knaves, as they went forth; because they carried
[Exit Cardinal] Are themselves always along with them.
you gone? Some fellows, they say, are possessed with the
evil, but this great fellow were able to possess the greatest
devil and make him worse.

ANTONIO.

He hath denied thee some suit?

BOSOLA.

He and his brother are like plum trees, that grow
crooked over standing pools, they are rich, and o’erladen
with fruit, but none but crows, pies, and caterpillars feed
on them. Could I be one of their flatt’ring panders, I would
hang on their ears like a horse-leech, till I were full, and
then drop off. I pray leave me. Who would rely upon these
miserable dependences, in expectation to be advanced
tomorrow? What creature ever fed worse, than hoping
Tantalus; nor ever died any man more fearfully, than he
that hoped for a pardon? There are rewards for hawks, and
dogs, when they have done us service; but for a soldier, that
hazards his limbs in a battle, nothing but a kind of geo-
metry is his last supportation.

DELIO.

Geometry?

BOSOLA.

Ay, to hang in a fair pair of slings, take his latter
swing in the world, upon an honourable pair of crutches,
from hospital to hospital: fare ye well sir. And yet do not
you scorn us, for places in the court are but like beds in the
hospital, where this man’s head lies at that man’s foot, and
so lower and lower.

[Exit BOSOLA.]

DELIO.

69I knew this fellow seven years in the galleys,
70For a notorious murther, and ’twas thought
71The Cardinal suborned it: he was released
72By the French general, Gaston de Foix
73When he recovered Naples.

ANTONIO.

When he recovered Naples. ’Tis great pity
74He should be thus neglected, I have heard
75He’s very valiant. This foul melancholy
76Will poison all his goodness, for, I’ll tell you,
77If too immoderate sleep be truly said
78To be an inward rust unto the soul;
79It then doth follow want of action
80Breeds all black malcontents, and their close rearing,
81Like moths in cloth, do hurt for want of wearing.

Scene ii

[Enter Castruchio, Silvio, Roderigo, and Grisolan.]

DELIO.

1The presence ’gins to fill. You promised me
2To make me the partaker of the natures
3Of some of your great courtiers.

ANTONIO.

Of some of your great courtiers. The Lord Cardinal’s
4And other strangers’, that are now in court?
5I shall. Here comes the great Calabrian Duke.

[Enter Ferdinand.]

FERDINAND.

6Who took the ring oft’nest?

SILVIO.

Who took the ring oft’nest? Antonio Bologna, my lord.

FERDINAND.

Our sister Duchess’ great master of her house-
hold? Give him the jewel: when shall we leave this sportive
action, and fall to action indeed?

CASTRUCHIO.

Methinks, my lord, you should not desire to
go to war, in person.

FERDINAND.

[aside]. Now, for some gravity: why, my lord?

CASTRUCHIO.

It is fitting a soldier arise to be a prince, but
not necessary a prince descend to be a captain!

FERDINAND.

No?

CASTRUCHIO.

No, my lord, he were far better do it by a
deputy.

FERDINAND.

Why should he not as well sleep, or eat, by a
deputy? This might take idle, offensive, and base office from
him, whereas the other deprives him of honour.

CASTRUCHIO.

Believe my experience: that realm is never
long in quiet, where the ruler is a soldier.

FERDINAND.

Thou told’st me thy wife could not endure
fighting.

CASTRUCHIO.

True, my lord.

FERDINAND.

And of a jest she broke, of a captain she met
full of wounds: I have forgot it.

CASTRUCHIO.

She told him, my lord, he was a pitiful fellow,
to lie, like the children of Ismael, all in tents.

FERDINAND.

Why, there’s a wit were able to undo all the
chirurgeons o’ the city, for although gallants should quarrel,
and had drawn their weapons, and were ready to go to it;
yet her persuasions would make them put up.

CASTRUCHIO.

That she would, my lord.
How do you like my Spanish jennet?

RODERIGO.

He is all fire.

FERDINAND.

I am of Pliny’s opinion, I think he was begot
by the wind; he runs as if he were ballasted with quick-
silver.

SILVIO.

True, my lord, he reels from the tilt often.

RODERIGO and DELIO.

Ha, ha, ha!

FERDINAND.

Why do you laugh? Methinks you that are
courtiers should be my touchwood, take fire when I give
fire; that is, laugh when I laugh, were the subject never so
witty,-

CASTRUCHIO.

True, my lord, I myself have heard a very
good jest, and have scorned to seem to have so silly a wit, as
to understand it.

FERDINAND.

But I can laugh at your fool, my lord.

CASTRUCHIO.

He cannot speak, you know, but he makes
faces; my lady cannot abide him.

FERDINAND.

No?

CASTRUCHIO.

Nor endure to be in merry company: for she
says too much laughing, and too much company, fills her
too full of the wrinkle.

FERDINAND.

I would then have a mathematical instrument
made for her face, that she might not laugh out of compass.
I shall shortly visit you at Milan, Lord Silvio.

SILVIO.

Your Grace shall arrive most welcome.

FERDINAND.

You are a good horseman, Antonio; you have
excellent riders in France, what do you think of good
horsemanship?

ANTONIO.

Nobly, my lord: as out of the Grecian horse
issued many famous princes: so out of brave horsemanship,
arise the first sparks of growing resolution, that raise the
mind to noble action.

FERDINAND.

You have bespoke it worthily.

[Enter Duchess, Cardinal, Cariola and Julia.]

SILVIO.

Your brother, the Lord Cardinal, and sister
Duchess.

CARDINAL.

Are the galleys come about?

DELIO.

They are, my lord.

FERDINAND.

Here’s the Lord Silvio, is come to take his
leave.

DELIO

[aside to Antonio]. Now, sir, your promise: what’s
that Cardinal? I mean his temper? They say he’s a brave
fellow, will play his five thousand crowns at tennis, dance,
court ladies, and one that hath fought single combats.

ANTONIO.

Some such flashes superficially hang on him, for
form: but observe his inward character: he is a melancholy
churchman. The spring in his face is nothing but the engen-
d’ring of toads: where he is jealous of any man, he lays
worse plots for them, than ever was imposed on Hercules:
for he strews in his way flatterers, panders, intelligencers,
atheists: and a thousand such political monsters: he
should have been Pope: but instead of coming to it by the
primitive decency of the Church, he did bestow bribes, so
largely, and so impudently, as if he would have carried it
away without Heaven’s knowledge. Some good he hath done.

DELIO.

89You have given too much of him: what’s his brother?

ANTONIO.

90The Duke there? a most perverse and turbulent nature;
91What appears in him mirth, is merely outside,
92If he laugh heartily, it is to laugh
93All honesty out of fashion.

DELIO.

All honesty out of fashion. Twins?

ANTONIO.

All honesty out of fashion. Twins? In quality:
94He speaks with others’ tongues, and hears men’s suits
95With others’ ears: will seem to sleep o’th’bench
96Only to entrap offenders in their answers;
97Dooms men to death by information,
98Rewards, by hearsay.

DELIO.

Rewards, by hearsay. Then the law to him
99Is like a foul black cobweb to a spider,
100He makes it his dwelling, and a prison
101To entangle those shall feed him.

ANTONIO.

To entangle those shall feed him. Most true:
102He nev’r pays debts, unless they be shrewd turns,
103And those he will confess, that he doth owe.
104Last: for his brother, there, the Cardinal,
105They that do flatter him most, say oracles
106Hang at his lips: and verily I believe them:
107For the devil speaks in them.
108But for their sister, the right noble Duchess,
109You never fixed your eye on three fair medals,
110Cast in one figure, of so different temper.
111For her discourse, it is so full of rapture
112You only will begin, then to be sorry
113When she doth end her speech: and wish, in wonder,
114She held it less vainglory to talk much
115Than your penance, to hear her: whilst she speaks,
116She throws upon a man so sweet a look,
117That it were able to raise one to a galliard
118That lay in a dead palsy; and to dote
119On that sweet countenance: but in that look
120There speaketh so divine a continence
121As cuts off all lascivious, and vain hope.
122Her days are practiced in such noble virtue,
123That, sure her nights, nay more, her very sleeps,
124Are more in heaven, than other ladies’ shrifts.
125Let all sweet ladies break their flatt’ring glasses,
126And dress themselves in her.

DELIO.

And dress themselves in her. Fie Antonio,
127You play the wire-drawer with her commendations.

ANTONIO.

128I’ll case the picture up: only thus much:
129All her particular worth grows to this sum:
130She stains the time past: lights the time to come.

CARIOLA.

131You must attend my lady, in the gallery,
132Some half an hour hence.

ANTONIO.

Some half an hour hence. I shall.

[Exeunt Antonio and Delio.]

FERDINAND.

133Sister, I have a suit to you.

DUCHESS.

Sister, I have a suit to you. To me, sir?

FERDINAND.

134A gentleman here: Daniel de Bosola:
135One, that was in the galleys.

DUCHESS.

One, that was in the galleys. Yes, I know him.

FERDINAND.

136A worthy fellow h’ is: pray let me entreat for
137The provisorship of your horse.

DUCHESS.

The provisorship of your horse. Your knowledge of him
138Commends him, and prefers him.

FERDINAND.

Commends him, and prefers him. Call him hither.
139[Exit attendant] We are now upon parting. Good Lord Silvio
140Do us commend to all our noble friends
141At the leaguer.

SILVIO.

At the leaguer. Sir, I shall.

DUCHESS.

At the leaguer. Sir, I shall. You are for Milan?

SILVIO.

At the leaguer. Sir, I shall. You are for Milan? I am.

DUCHESS.

142Bring the caroches: we’ll bring you down to the haven.

[Exeunt Dutchess, Cariola, Silvio, Castruchio, Roderigo, Grisolan and Julia.]

CARDINAL.

143Be sure you entertain that Bosola
144For your intelligence: I would not be seen in’t.
145And therefore many times I have slighted him,
146When he did court our furtherance: as this morning.

FERDINAND.

147Antonio, the great master of her household
148Had been far fitter.

CARDINAL.

Had been far fitter. You are deceived in him,
149His nature is too honest for such business.
150He comes: I’ll leave you.

[Enter Bosola]

BOSOLA.

He comes: I’ll leave you. I was lured to you.

[Exit Cardinal.]

FERDINAND.

151My brother here, the Cardinal, could never
152Abide you.

BOSOLA.

Abide you. Never since he was in my debt.

FERDINAND.

153May be some oblique character in your face
154Made him suspect you?

BOSOLA.

Made him suspect you? Doth he study physiognomy?
155There’s no more credit to be given to th’face,
156Than to a sick man’s urine, which some call
157The physician’s whore, because she cozens him.
158He did suspect me wrongfully.

FERDINAND.

He did suspect me wrongfully. For that
159You must give great men leave to take their times:
160Distrust doth cause us seldom be deceived;
161You see, the oft shaking of the cedar tree
162Fastens it more at root.

BOSOLA.

Fastens it more at root. Yet take heed:
163For to suspect a friend unworthily
164Instructs him the next way to suspect you,
165And prompts him to deceive you.

FERDINAND .

And prompts him to deceive you. There’s gold.

BOSOLA.

And prompts him to deceive you. There’s gold. So:
166What follows? (Never rained such showers as these
167Without thunderbolts i’th’tail of them;)
168Whose throat must I cut?

FERDINAND.

169Your inclination to shed blood rides post
170Before my occasion to use you. I give you that
171To live i’th’ court, here: and observe the Duchess,
172To note all the particulars of her haviour:
173What suitors do solicit her for marriage
174And whom she best affects: she’s a young widow,
175I would not have her marry again.

BOSOLA.

I would not have her marry again. No, sir?

FERDINAND.

176Do not you ask the reason: but be satisfied,
177I say I would not.

BOSOLA.

I say I would not. It seems you would create me
178One of your familiars.

FERDINAND .

One of your familiars. Familiar? what’s that?

BOSOLA.

179Why, a very quaint invisible devil in flesh:
180An intelligencer.

FERDINAND .

An intelligencer. Such a kind of thriving thing
181I would wish thee: and ere long, thou mayst arrive
182At a higher place by’t.

BOSOLA.

At a higher place by’t. Take your devils
183Which hell calls angels: these cursed gifts would make
184You a corrupter, me an impudent traitor,
185And should I take these, they’ll’d take me to hell.

FERDINAND.

186Sir, I’ll take nothing from you that I have given.
187There is a place that I procured for you
188This morning, the provisorship o’th’horse,
189Have you heard on’t?

BOSOLA.

Have you heard on’t? No.

FERDINAND .

Have you heard on’t? No. ’Tis yours, is’t not worth thanks?

BOSOLA.

190I would have you curse yourself now, that your bounty,
191Which makes men truly noble, e’er should make
192Me a villain: oh, that to avoid ingratitude
193For the good deed you have done me, I must do
194All the ill man can invent. Thus the devil
195Candies all sins o’er: and what heaven terms vild,
196That names he complemental.

FERDINAND.

That names he complemental. Be yourself:
197Keep your old garb of melancholy: ’twill express
198You envy those that stand above your reach,
199Yet strive not to come near ’em. This will gain
200Access to private lodgings, where yourself
201May, like a politic dormouse,—

BOSOLA.

May, like a politic dormouse,— As I have seen some,
202Feed in a lord’s dish, half asleep, not seeming
203To listen to any talk: and yet these rogues
204Have cut his throat in a dream: what’s my place?
205The provisorship o’th’ horse? say then my corruption
206Grew out of horse dung. I am your creature.

FERDINAND.

Grew out of horse dung. I am your creature. Away!

BOSOLA.

207Let good men, for good deeds, covet good fame,
208Since place and riches oft are bribes of shame;
209Sometimes the devil doth preach.

Exit Bosola.

[Enter Cardinal, Duchess and Cariola.]

CARDINAL.

210We are to part from you: and your own discretion
211Must now be your director.

FERDINAND.

Must now be your director. You are a widow:
212You know already what man is: and therefore
213Let not youth: high promotion, eloquence,—

CARDINAL.

214No, nor anything without the addition, Honour,
215Sway your high blood.

FERDINAND.

Sway your high blood. Marry? They are most luxurious,
216Will wed twice.

CARDINAL.

Will wed twice. Oh, fie!

FERDINAND .

Will wed twice. Oh, fie! Their livers are more spotted
217Than Laban’s sheep.

DUCHESS.

Than Laban’s sheep. Diamonds are of most value
218They say, that have passed through most jewellers’ hands.

FERDINAND.

219Whores, by that rule, are precious.

DUCHESS.

220Will you hear me?
Will you hear me? I’ll never marry―

CARDINAL.

Will you hear me? I’ll never marry― So most widows say:
221But commonly that motion lasts no longer
222Than the turning of an hourglass; the funeral sermon
223And it, end both together.

FERDINAND.

And it, end both together. Now hear me:
224You live in a rank pasture here, i’th’ court,
225There is a kind of honeydew that’s deadly:
226’Twill poison your fame; look to’t; be not cunning:
227For they whose faces do belie their hearts
228Are witches, ere they arrive at twenty years,
229Ay: and give the devil suck.

DUCHESS.

Ay: and give the devil suck. This is terrible good counsel.

FERDINAND.

230Hypocrisy is woven of a fine small thread,
231Subtler than Vulcan’s engine: yet, believe’t,
232Your darkest actions: nay, your privat’st thoughts,
233Will come to light.

CARDINAL.

Will come to light. You may flatter yourself,
234And take your own choice: privately be married
235Under the eaves of night―

FERDINAND.

Under the eaves of night― Think’t the best voyage
236That e’er you made; like the irregular crab,
237Which, though ’t goes backward, thinks that it goes right,
238Because it goes its own way: but observe:
239Such weddings may more properly be said
240To be executed, than celebrated.

CARDINAL.

To be executed, than celebrated. The marriage night
241Is the entrance into some prison.

FERDINAND.

Is the entrance into some prison. And those joys,
242Those lustful pleasures, are like heavy sleeps
243Which do forerun man’s mischief.

CARDINAL.

Which do forerun man’s mischief. Fare you well.
244Wisdom begins at the end: remember it.

[Exit Cardinal.]

DUCHESS.

245I think this speech between you both was studied,
246It came so roundly off.

FERDINAND.

It came so roundly off. You are my sister.
247This was my father’s poniard: do you see,
248I’ll’d be loath to see’t look rusty, ’cause ’twas his.
249I would have you to give o’er these chargeable revels;
250A visor and a mask are whispering-rooms
251That were nev’r built for goodness: fare ye well:
252And women like that part, which, like the lamprey,
253Hath nev’r a bone in’t.

DUCHESS.

Hath nev’r a bone in’t. Fie, sir!

FERDINAND .

Hath nev’r a bone in’t. Fie, sir! Nay,
254I mean the tongue: variety of courtship;
255What cannot a neat knave with a smooth tale
256Make a woman believe? Farewell, lusty widow.

[Exit Ferdinand.]

DUCHESS.

257Shall this move me? If all my royal kindred
258Lay in my way unto this marriage:
259I’ll’d make them my low foot-steps. And even now,
260Even in this hate, (as men in some great battles
261By apprehending danger, have achieved
262Almost impossible actions: I have heard soldiers say so,)
263So I, through frights and threat’nings, will assay
264This dangerous venture. Let old wives report
265I winked, and chose a husband. Cariola,
266To thy known secrecy I have given up
267More than my life, my fame.

CARIOLA.

More than my life, my fame. Both shall be safe:
268For I’ll conceal this secret from the world
269As warily as those that trade in poison,
270Keep poison from their children.

DUCHESS.

Keep poison from their children. Thy protestation
271Is ingenious and hearty. I believe it.
272Is Antonio come?

CARIOLA.

Is Antonio come? He attends you.

DUCHESS.

Is Antonio come? He attends you. Good dear soul,
273Leave me: but place thyself behind the arras,
274Where thou mayst overhear us: wish me good speed,
275For I am going into a wilderness,
276Where I shall find nor path, nor friendly clew
277To be my guide.
To be my guide. [Cariola goes behind the arras; the Dutchess draws the traverse to reveal Antonio.] I sent for you. Sit down:
278Take pen and ink, and write. Are you ready?

ANTONIO.

279Yes.

DUCHESS.

Yes. What did I say?

ANTONIO.

280That I should write somewhat.

DUCHESS.

That I should write somewhat. Oh, I remember:
281After these triumphs and this large expense
282It’s fit, like thrifty husbands, we inquire
283What’s laid up for tomorrow.

ANTONIO.

284So please your beauteous excellence.

DUCHESS.

So please your beauteous excellence. Beauteous?
285Indeed I thank you: I look young for your sake.
286You have tane my cares upon you.

ANTONIO.

You have tane my cares upon you. I’ll fetch your Grace
287The particulars of your revenue and expense.

DUCHESS.

288Oh, you are an upright treasurer: but you mistook,
289For when I said I meant to make inquiry
290What’s laid up for tomorrow: I did mean
291What’s laid up yonder for me.

ANTONIO.

What’s laid up yonder for me. Where?

DUCHESS.

What’s laid up yonder for me. Where? In heaven.
292I am making my will, as ’tis fit princes should
293In perfect memory, and I pray sir, tell me
294Were not one better make it smiling, thus?
295Than in deep groans, and terrible ghastly looks,
296As if the gifts we parted with, procured
297That violent distraction?

ANTONIO.

That violent distraction? Oh, much better.

DUCHESS.

298If I had a husband now, this care were quit:
299But I intend to make you overseer;
300What good deed shall we first remember? Say.

ANTONIO.

301Begin with that first good deed, began i’th’ world,
302After man’s creation, the sacrament of marriage.
303I’ld have you first provide for a good husband,
304Give him all.

DUCHESS.

Give him all. All?

ANTONIO.

Give him all. All? Yes, your excellent self.

DUCHESS.

305In a winding-sheet?

ANTONIO.

In a winding-sheet? In a couple.

DUCHESS.

306St. Winifred! that were a strange will.

ANTONIO.

St. Winifred! that were a strange will. ’Twere strange
307If there were no will in you to marry again.

DUCHESS.

308What do you think of marriage?

ANTONIO.

309I take’t, as those that deny purgatory,
310It locally contains or heaven, or hell;
311There’s no third place in’t.

DUCHESS.

There’s no third place in’t. How do you affect it?

ANTONIO.

312My banishment, feeding my melancholy,
313Would often reason thus: —

DUCHESS.

Would often reason thus: — Pray let’s hear it.

ANTONIO.

314Say a man never marry, nor have children,
315What takes that from him? Only the bare name
316Of being a father, or the weak delight
317To see the little wanton ride a-cock-horse
318Upon a painted stick, or hear him chatter
319Like a taught starling.

DUCHESS.

Like a taught starling. Fie, fie, what’s all this?
320One of your eyes is bloodshot, use my ring to’t,
321They say ’tis very sovereign: ’twas my wedding ring,
322And I did vow never to part with it,
323But to my second husband.

ANTONIO.

But to my second husband. You have parted with it now.

DUCHESS.

324Yes, to help your eyesight.

ANTONIO.

Yes, to help your eyesight. You have made me stark blind.

DUCHESS.

Yes, to help your eyesight. You have made me stark blind. How?

ANTONIO.

325There is a saucy and ambitious devil
326Is dancing in this circle.

DUCHESS.

Is dancing in this circle. Remove him.

ANTONIO.

Is dancing in this circle. Remove him. How?

DUCHESS.

327There needs small conjuration, when your finger
328May do it: thus, is it fit?

[She puts the ring on his finger.] he kneels.

ANTONIO.

May do it: thus, is it fit? What said you?

DUCHESS.

May do it: thus, is it fit? What said you? Sir,
329This goodly roof of yours, is too low built,
330I cannot stand upright in’t, nor discourse,
331Without I raise it higher: raise yourself,
332Or, if you please, my hand to help you: so.

[Raises him.

ANTONIO.

333Ambition, Madam, is a great man’s madness,
334That is not kept in chains, and close-pent rooms,
335But in fair lightsome lodgings, and is girt
336With the wild noise of prattling visitants,
337Which makes it lunatic, beyond all cure.
338Conceive not, I am so stupid, but I aim
339Whereto your favours tend. But he’s a fool
340That, being a-cold, would thrust his hands i’th’ fire
341To warm them.

DUCHESS.

To warm them. So, now the ground’s broke,
342You may discover what a wealthy mine
343I make you lord of.

ANTONIO.

I make you lord of. Oh, my unworthiness!

DUCHESS.

344You were ill to sell yourself;
345This dark’ning of your worth is not like that
346Which tradesmen use i’th’ city; their false lights
347Are to rid bad wares off: and I must tell you
348If you will know where breathes a complete man,
349(I speak it without flattery), turn your eyes,
350And progress through yourself.

ANTONIO.

351Were there nor heaven, nor hell,
352I should be honest: I have long served virtue,
353And nev’r tane wages of her.

DUCHESS.

And nev’r tane wages of her. Now she pays it.
354The misery of us, that are born great,
355We are forced to woo, because none dare woo us:
356And as a tyrant doubles with his words,
357And fearfully equivocates: so we
358Are forced to express our violent passions
359In riddles, and in dreams, and leave the path
360Of simple virtue, which was never made
361To seem the thing it is not. Go, go brag
362You have left me heartless, mine is in your bosom,
363I hope ’twill multiply love there. You do tremble:
364Make not your heart so dead a piece of flesh
365To fear, more than to love me. Sir, be confident,
366What is’t distracts you? This is flesh, and blood, sir,
367’Tis not the figure cut in alabaster
368Kneels at my husband’s tomb. Awake, awake, man,
369I do here put off all vain ceremony,
370And only do appear to you, a young widow
371That claims you for her husband, and like a widow,
372I use but half a blush in’t.

ANTONIO.

I use but half a blush in’t. Truth speak for me,
373I will remain the constant sanctuary
374Of your good name.

DUCHESS.

Of your good name. I thank you, gentle love,
375And ’cause you shall not come to me in debt,
376Being now my steward, here upon your lips
377I sign your Quietus est. This you should have begged now:
378I have seen children oft eat sweetmeats thus,
379As fearful to devour them too soon.

ANTONIO.

380But for your brothers?

DUCHESS.

But for your brothers? Do not think of them:
381All discord, without this circumference,
382Is only to be pitied, and not feared.
383Yet, should they know it, time will easily
384Scatter the tempest.

ANTONIO.

Scatter the tempest. These words should be mine,
385And all the parts you have spoke, if some part of it
386Would not have savored flattery.

DUCHESS.

Would not have savored flattery. Kneel.

[Enter Cariola.]

ANTONIO.

Would not have savored flattery. Kneel. Ha?

DUCHESS.

387Be not amazed, this woman’s of my counsel.
388I have heard lawyers say, a contract in a chamber,
389Per verba de presenti, is absolute marriage.
390[The Duchess and Antonio kneel.] Bless, Heaven, this sacred Gordian, which let violence
[The Duchess and Antonio kneel.] Bless, Heaven, this sacred Gordian, which let violence Never untwine.

ANTONIO.

391And may our sweet affections, like the spheres,
392Be still in motion.

DUCHESS.

Be still in motion. Quick’ning, and make
Be still in motion. Quick’ning, and make The like soft music.

ANTONIO.

393That we may imitate the loving palms,
394Best emblem of a peaceful marriage,
395That nev’r bore fruit divided.

DUCHESS.

396What can the Church force more?

ANTONIO.

397That Fortune may not know an accident
398Either of joy or sorrow, to divide
399Our fixèd wishes.

DUCHESS.

400How can the church build faster?
401We now are man and wife, and ’tis the Church
402That must but echo this. Maid, stand apart.
403I now am blind.

ANTONIO.

I now am blind. What’s your conceit in this?

DUCHESS.

404I would have you lead your fortune by the hand,
405Unto your marriage bed:

(You speak in me this, for we now are one)

406We’ll only lie, and talk together, and plot
407T’appease my humorous kindred; and, if you please,
408Like the old tale, in Alexander and Lodowick,
409Lay a naked sword between us, keep us chaste.
410Oh, let me shroud my blushes in your bosom,
411Since ’tis the treasury of all my secrets.

CARIOLA.

412Whether the spirit of greatness, or of woman
413Reign most in her, I know not, but it shows
414A fearful madness: I owe her much of pity.

Exeunt.

Act II

Scene i

[Enter Bosola and Castruchio.]

BOSOLA.

You say you would fain be taken for an eminent
courtier?

CASTRUCHIO.

‘Tis the very main of my ambition.

BOSOLA.

Let me see, you have a reasonable good face for’t
already, and your nightcap expresses your ears sufficient
largely; I would have you learn to twirl the strings of your
band with a good grace; and in a set speech, at th’ end of
every sentence, to hum, three or four times, or blow your
nose, till it smart again, to recover your memory. When
you come to be a president in criminal causes, if you smile
upon a prisoner, hang him, but if you frown upon him, and
threaten him, let him be sure to scape the gallows.

CASTRUCHIO.

I would be a very merry president,―

BOSOLA.

Do not sup a nights; ’twill beget you an admirable
wit.

CASTRUCHIO.

Rather it would make me have a good stomach
to quarrel, for they say your roaring boys eat meat seldom,
and that makes them so valiant: but how shall I know
whether the people take me for an eminent fellow?

BOSOLA.

I will teach a trick to know it: give out you lie a-
dying, and if you hear the common people curse you, be
sure you are taken for one of the prime nightcaps. [Enter Old Lady]
You come from painting now?

OLD LADY.

From what?

BOSOLA.

Why, from your scurvy face physic: To behold
thee not painted inclines somewhat near a miracle. These
in thy face here, were deep ruts and foul sloughs, the last
progress. There was a lady in France, that having had the
smallpox, flayed the skin off her face, to make it more level;
and whereas before she looked like a nutmeg grater, after
she resembled an abortive hedgehog.

OLD LADY.

Do you call this painting?

BOSOLA.

No, no but you call it careening of an old mor-
phewed lady, to make her disembogue again. There’s rough-
cast phrase to your plastic.

OLD LADY.

It seems you are well acquainted with my
closet?

BOSOLA.

One would suspect it for a shop of witchcraft,
to find in it the fat of serpents; spawn of snakes, Jews’
spittle, and their young children’s ordure, and all these for
the face. I would sooner eat a dead pigeon, taken from the soles
of the feet of one sick of the plague, than kiss one of you
fasting. Here are two of you, whose sin of your youth is the
very patrimony of the physician, makes him renew his
footcloth with the spring, and change his high-prized
courtesan with the fall of the leaf: I do wonder you do not
loathe yourselves. Observe my meditation now:

48What thing is in this outward form of man
49To be beloved? We account it ominous,
50If nature do produce a colt, or lamb,
51A fawn, or goat, in any limb resembling
52A man; and fly from’t as a prodigy.
53Man stands amazed to see his deformity,
54In any other creature but himself.
55But in our own flesh, though we bear diseases
56Which have their true names only tane from beasts,
57As the most ulcerous wolf, and swinish measle;
58Though we are eaten up of lice, and worms,
59And though continually we bear about us
60A rotten and dead body, we delight
61To hide it in rich tissue: all our fear,
62Nay, all our terror, is lest our physician
63Should put us in the ground, to be made sweet,
64Your wife’s gone to Rome: you two couple, and get you
65To the wells at Lucca, to recover your aches.

[Exeunt Castruchio and Old Lady.]

66I have other work on foot: I observe our Duchess
67Is sick a-days, she pukes, her stomach seethes,
68The fins of her eyelids look most teeming blue,
69She wanes i’th’ cheek, and waxes fat i’th’ flank;
70And, contrary to our Italian fashion,
71Wears a loose-bodied gown: there’s somewhat in’t.
72I have a trick, may chance discover it,
73A pretty one; I have bought some apricocks,
74The first our spring yields.

[Enter Antonio and Delio]

DELIO.

The first our spring yields. And so long since married?
75You amaze me.

ANTONIO.

You amaze me. Let me seal your lips for ever,
76For did I think that anything but th’ air
77Could carry these words from you, I should wish
78You had no breath at all.
You had no breath at all. [To Bosola] Now sir, in your contemplation?
79You are studying to become a great wise fellow?

BOSOLA.

Oh sir, the opinion of wisdom is a foul tetter,
that runs all over a man’s body: if simplicity direct us to
have no evil, it directs us to a happy being. For the subtlest
folly proceeds from the subtlest wisdom. Let me be simply
honest.

ANTONIO.

I do understand your inside.

BOSOLA.

Do you so?

ANTONIO.

87Because you would not seem to appear to th’ world
88Puffed up with your preferment, you continue
89This out of fashion melancholy; leave it, leave it.

BOSOLA.

Give me leave to be honest in any phrase, in any
compliment whatsoever: shall I confess myself to you? I
look no higher than I can reach: they are the gods, that
must ride on winged horses, a lawyer’s mule of a slow pace
will both suit my disposition and business. For, mark me,
when a man’s mind rides faster than his horse can gallop
they quickly both tire.

ANTONIO.

97You would look up to Heaven, but I think
98The devil, that rules i’th’ air, stands in your light.

BOSOLA.

Oh, sir, you are lord of the ascendant, chief man
with the Duchess: a duke was your cousin-german,
removed. Say you were lineally descended from King
Pippin, or he himself, what of this? Search the heads of the
greatest rivers in the world, you shall find them but bubbles
of water. Some would think the souls of princes were
brought forth by some more weighty cause, than those of
meaner persons; they are deceived, there’s the same hand to
them: the like passions sway them: the same reason, that
makes a vicar go to law for a tithe-pig, and undo his neigh-
bours, makes them spoil a whole province, and batter down
goodly cities with the cannon.

[Enter Duchess, Old Lady, Ladies.]

DUCHESS.

111Your arm Antonio, do I not grow fat?
112I am exceeding short-winded. Bosola,
113I would have you, sir, provide for me a litter,
114Such a one, as the Duchess of Florence rode in.

BOSOLA.

115The duchess used one, when she was great with child.

DUCHESS.

116I think she did. Come hither, mend my ruff,
117Here; when? thou art such a tedious lady; and
118Thy breath smells of lemon peels; would thou hadst done;
119Shall I sound under thy fingers? I am
120So troubled with the mother.

BOSOLA.

So troubled with the mother. [aside]. I fear too much.aparte

DUCHESS.

121I have heard you say that the French courtiers
122Wear their hats on ’fore the king.

ANTONIO.

123I have seen it.

DUCHESS.

I have seen it. In the presence?

ANTONIO.

I have seen it. In the presence? Yes:

DUCHESS.

124Why should not we bring up that fashion?
125’Tis ceremony more than duty, that consists
126In the removing of a piece of felt:
127Be you the example to the rest o’th’ court,
128Put on your hat first.

ANTONIO.

Put on your hat first. You must pardon me:
129I have seen, in colder countries than in France,
130Nobles stand bare to th’ prince; and the distinction
131Methought showed reverently.

BOSOLA.

Methought showed reverently. I have a present for your Grace.

DUCHESS.

132For me, sir?

BOSOLA.

For me, sir? Apricocks, Madam.

DUCHESS.

For me, sir? Apricocks, Madam. Oh sir, where are they?
133I have heard of none to-year.

BOSOLA.

I have heard of none to-year. [aside]. Good, her colour rises.aparte

DUCHESS.

134Indeed I thank you: they are wondrous fair ones.
135What an unskilful fellow is our gardener!
136We shall have none this month.

BOSOLA.

137Will not your Grace pare them?

DUCHESS.

138No, they taste of musk, methinks; indeed they do.

BOSOLA.

139I know not: yet I wish your Grace had pared ’em.

DUCHESS.

140Why?

BOSOLA.

Why? I forget to tell you the knave gard’ner,
141Only to raise his profit by them the sooner,
142Did ripen them in horse-dung.

DUCHESS.

Did ripen them in horse-dung. Oh you jest.
143[to Antonio] You shall judge: pray taste one.

ANTONIO.

[to Antonio] You shall judge: pray taste one. Indeed Madam,
144I do not love the fruit.

DUCHESS.

I do not love the fruit. Sir, you are loath
145To rob us of our dainties: ’tis a delicate fruit,
146They say they are restorative?

BOSOLA.

147’Tis a pretty art,
’Tis a pretty art, This grafting.

DUCHESS.

’Tis a pretty art, This grafting. ’Tis so: a bett’ring of nature.

BOSOLA.

148To make a pippin grow upon a crab,
149A damson on a black-thorn:
A damson on a black-thorn: [aside] How greedily she eats them!aparte
150A whirlwind strike off these bawd farthingales,
151For, but for that, and the loose-bodied gown,
152I should have discovered apparently
153The young springal cutting a caper in her belly.

DUCHESS.

154I thank you, Bosola: they were right good ones,
155If they do not make me sick.

ANTONIO.

If they do not make me sick. How now Madam?

DUCHESS.

156This green fruit: and my stomach are not friends.
157How they swell me!

BOSOLA

How they swell me! [aside]. Nay, you are too much swelled already.aparte

DUCHESS.

158Oh, I am in an extreme cold sweat.

BOSOLA.

Oh, I am in an extreme cold sweat. I am very sorry.

[Exit]

DUCHESS.

159Lights to my chamber! O, good Antonio,
160I fear I am undone.

Exit Duchess.

DELIO.

I fear I am undone. Lights there, lights!

ANTONIO.

161O my most trusty Delio, we are lost:
162I fear she’s fall’n in labour: and there’s left
163No time for her remove.

DELIO.

No time for her remove. Have you prepared
164Those ladies to attend her? and procured
165That politic safe conveyance for the midwife
166Your duchess plotted?

ANTONIO.

Your duchess plotted? I have.

DELIO.

167Make use then of this forced occasion:
168Give out that Bosola hath poisoned her,
169With these apricocks: that will give some colour
170For her keeping close.

ANTONIO.

For her keeping close. Fie, fie, the physicians
171Will then flock to her.

DELIO.

Will then flock to her. For that you may pretend
172She’ll use some prepared antidote of her own,
173Lest the physicians should repoison her.

ANTONIO.

174I am lost in amazement: I know not what to think on’t.

Ex[eunt].

Scene ii

[Enter Bosola and Old Lady]

BOSOLA.

So, so: there’s no question but her tetchiness and
most vulturous eating of the apricots, are apparent signs
of breeding, now?

OLD LADY.

I am in haste, sir.

BOSOLA.

There was a young waiting-woman, had a
monstrous desire to see the glass-house―

OLD LADY.

Nay, pray let me go:

BOSOLA.

And it was only to know what strange instrument
it was, should swell up a glass to the fashion of a woman’s
belly.

OLD LADY.

I will hear no more of the glass-house, you are
still abusing women?

BOSOLA.

Who, I? no, only, by the way now and then,
mention your frailties. The orange tree bears ripe and
green fruit and blossoms altogether. And some of you give
entertainment for pure love: but more, for more precious
reward. The lusty spring smells well: but drooping autumn
tastes well. If we have the same golden showers, that rained
in the time of Jupiter the Thunderer: you have the same
Danaes still, to hold up their laps to receive them: didst
thou never study the mathematics?

OLD LADY.

What’s that, sir?

BOSOLA.

Why, to know the trick how to make a many lines
meet in one centre. Go, go; give your foster-daughters good
counsel: tell them, that the devil takes delight to hang at a
woman’s girdle, like a false rusty watch, that she cannot
discern how the time passes.

[Exit Old Lady; enter Antonio, Delio, Roderigo, Grisolan.]

ANTONIO.

28Shut up the court gates.

RODERIGO.

29Why sir? what’s the danger?

ANTONIO.

30Shut up the posterns presently: and call
31All the officers o’th’ court.

GRISOLAN.

All the officers o’th’ court. I shall instantly.

[Exit.

ANTONIO.

32Who keeps the key o’th’ park-gate?

RODERIGO.

33Forobosco.

ANTONIO.

Forobosco. Let him bring’t presently.

[Exit Roderigo.

[Enter servants, Grisolan, Roderigo.]

1 SERVANT.

34Oh, gentlemen o’th’ court, the foulest treason!

BOSOLA

35[aside]. If that these apricocks should be poisoned, now;aparte
36Without my knowledge!

1 SERVANT.

Without my knowledge! There was taken even now
37A Switzer in the Duchess’ bedchamber.

2 SERVANT.

38A Switzer?

1 SERVANT.

A Switzer? With a pistol in his great cod-piece.

BOSOLA.

39Ha, ha, ha.

1 SERVANT.

40The cod-piece was the case for’t.

2 SERVANT.

41There was a cunning traitor.
42Who would have searched his cod-piece?

1 SERVANT.

43True, if he had kept out of the ladies’ chambers:
44And all the molds of his buttons were leaden bullets.

2 SERVANT.

45Oh wicked cannibal: a fire-lock in’s cod-piece?

1 SERVANT.

46’ Twas a French plot upon my life.

2 SERVANT.

47To see what the devil can do!

ANTONIO.

48All the officers here?

SERVANTS.

All the officers here? We are.

ANTONIO.

All the officers here? We are. Gentlemen,
49We have lost much plate you know; and but this evening
50Jewels, to the value of four thousand ducats
51Are missing in the Duchess’ cabinet.
52Are the gates shut?

1 SERVANT.

Are the gates shut? Yes.

ANTONIO.

Are the gates shut? Yes. ’Tis the Duchess’ pleasure
53Each officer be locked into his chamber
54Till the sun-rising; and to send the keys
55Of all their chests, and of their outward doors
56Into her bedchamber. She is very sick.

RODERIGO.

57At her pleasure.

ANTONIO.

58She entreats you take’t not ill. The innocent
59Shall be the more approved by it.

BOSOLA.

60Gentleman o’th’ wood-yard, where’s your Switzer now?

1 SERVANT.

By this hand ’twas credibly reported by one
o’th’ black-guard.

[Exeunt Bosola, Roderigo and Servants.]

DELIO.

63How fares it with the Duchess?

ANTONIO.

How fares it with the Duchess? She’s exposed
64Unto the worst of torture, pain, and fear.

DELIO.

65Speak to her all happy comfort.

ANTONIO.

66How I do play the fool with mine own danger!
67You are this night, dear friend, to post to Rome,
68My life lies in your service.

DELIO.

My life lies in your service. Do not doubt me.

ANTONIO.

69Oh, ’tis far from me: and yet fear presents me
70Somewhat that looks like danger.

DELIO.

Somewhat that looks like danger. Believe it,
71’Tis but the shadow of your fear, no more:
72How superstitiously we mind our evils!
73The throwing down salt, or crossing of a hare;
74Bleeding at nose, the stumbling of a horse:
75Or singing of a cricket, are of power
76To daunt whole man in us. Sir, fare you well:
77I wish you all the joys of a blessed father;
78And, for my faith, lay this unto your breast,
79Old friends, like old swords, still are trusted best.

[Exit Delio.]

[Enter Cariola with a child.]

CARIOLA.

80Sir, you are the happy father of a son,
81Your wife commends him to you.

ANTONIO.

Your wife commends him to you. Bless’d comfort!
82For heaven’ sake tend her well: I’ll presently
83Go set a figure for’s nativity.

Exeunt.

Scene iii

[Enter Bosola with a dark lanthorn.]

BOSOLA.

1Sure I did hear a woman shriek: list, Ha?
2And the sound came, if I received it right,
3From the Duchess’ lodgings: there’s some stratagem
4In the confining all our courtiers
5To their several wards. I must have part of it,
6My intelligence will freeze else. List again,
7It may be ’twas the melancholy bird,
8Best friend of silence, and of solitariness,
9The owl, that screamed so: ha! Antonio?

[Enter Antonio with a candle, his sword drawn.]

ANTONIO.

10I heard some noise: who’s there? What art thou? Speak.

BOSOLA.

11Antonio! Put not your face nor body
12To such a forced expression of fear,
13I am Bosola; your friend.

ANTONIO.

I am Bosola; your friend. Bosola?
14[aside] This mole does undermine me― heard you notaparte
15A noise even now?

BOSOLA.

A noise even now? From whence?

ANTONIO.

16From the Duchess’ lodging.

BOSOLA.

From the Duchess’ lodging. Not I: did you?

ANTONIO.

17I did: or else I dreamed.

BOSOLA.

I did: or else I dreamed. Let’s walk towards it.

ANTONIO.

I did: or else I dreamed. Let’s walk towards it. No. It may be ’twas
18But the rising of the wind.

BOSOLA.

But the rising of the wind. Very likely.
19Methinks ’tis very cold, and yet you sweat.
20You look wildly.

ANTONIO.

You look wildly. I have been setting a figure
21For the Duchess’ jewels.

BOSOLA.

For the Duchess’ jewels. Ah: and how falls your question?
22Do you find it radical?

ANTONIO.

Do you find it radical? What’s that to you?
23’Tis rather to be questioned what design,
24When all men were commanded to their lodgings,
25Makes you a night-walker.

BOSOLA.

Makes you a night-walker. In sooth I’ll tell you:
26Now all the court’s asleep, I thought the devil
27Had least to do here; I came to say my prayers,
28And if it do offend you, I do so,
29You are a fine courtier.

ANTONIO

You are a fine courtier. [aside]. This fellow will undo me.aparte
30You gave the Duchess apricocks to-day,
31Pray heaven they were not poisoned!

BOSOLA.

Pray heaven they were not poisoned! Poisoned? a Spanish fig
32For the imputation!

ANTONIO.

For the imputation! Traitors are ever confident,
33Till they are discovered. There were jewels stol’n too,
34In my conceit, none are to be suspected
35More than yourself.

BOSOLA.

More than yourself. You are a false steward.

ANTONIO.

36Saucy slave! I’ll pull thee up by the roots.

BOSOLA.

37May be the ruin will crush you to pieces.

ANTONIO.

38You are an impudent snake indeed, sir,
39Are you scarce warm, and do you show your sting?

BOSOLA.

40…

ANTONIO.

41You libel well, sir.

BOSOLA.

You libel well, sir. No, sir, copy it out:
42And I will set my hand to’t.

ANTONIO.

And I will set my hand to’t. My nose bleeds.
43One that were superstitious, would count
44This ominous: when it merely comes by chance.
45Two letters, that are wrought here for my name
46Are drowned in blood!
47Mere accident: for you, sir, I'll take order:
48I’th’ morn you shall be safe:
I’th’ morn you shall be safe: [aside] ’tis that must colouraparte
49Her lying-in: sir, this door you pass not:
50I do not hold it fit, that you come near
51The Duchess’ lodgings, till you have quit yourself;
52[aside] The great are like the base; nay, they are the same,aparte
53When they seek shameful ways to avoid shame.

Ex[it.]

BOSOLA.

54Antonio hereabout did drop a paper,
55Some of your help, false friend: oh, here it is.
56What’s here? a child’s nativity calculated?

[reads:] The Duchess was delivered of a son, ’tween the hours
twelve and one, in the night: Anno Dom: 1504. (that’s this
year) decimo nono Decembris (that’s this night) taken
according to the Meridian of Malfi (that’s our Duchess: happy
discovery). The Lord of the first house, being combust in the
ascendant, signifies short life: and Mars being in a human
sign, joined to the tail of the Dragon, in the eighth house, doth
threaten a violent death; Cætera non scrutantur.

65Why now ’tis most apparent. This precise fellow
66Is the Duchess’ bawd: I have it to my wish.
67This is a parcel of intelligency
68Our courtiers were cased up for! It needs must follow,
69That I must be committed, on pretence
70Of poisoning her: which I’ll endure, and laugh at.
71If one could find the father now: but that
72Time will discover. Old Castruchio
73I’th’ morning posts to Rome; by him I’ll send
74A letter, that shall make her brothers’ galls
75O’erflow their livers. This was a thrifty way!
76Though lust do masque in ne’er so strange disguise
77She’s oft found witty, but is never wise.

[Exit.]

Scene iv

[Enter Cardinal and Julia.]

CARDINAL.

1Sit: thou art my best of wishes; prithee tell me
2What trick didst thou invent to come to Rome,
3Without thy husband?

JULIA.

Without thy husband? Why, my Lord, I told him
4I came to visit an old anchorite
5Here, for devotion.

CARDINAL.

Here, for devotion. Thou art a witty false one:
6I mean to him.

JULIA.

I mean to him. You have prevailed with me
7Beyond my strongest thoughts: I would not now
8Find you inconstant.

CARDINAL.

Find you inconstant. Do not put thyself
9To such a voluntary torture, which proceeds
10Out of your own guilt.

JULIA.

Out of your own guilt. How, my Lord?

CARDINAL.

Out of your own guilt. How, my Lord? You fear
11My constancy, because you have approved
12Those giddy and wild turnings in yourself.

JULIA.

13Did you e’er find them?

CARDINAL.

Did you e’er find them? Sooth, generally for women;
14A man might strive to make glass malleable,
15Ere he should make them fixed.

JULIA.

Ere he should make them fixed. So, my Lord.

CARDINAL.

16We had need go borrow that fantastic glass
17Invented by Galileo the Florentine,
18To view another spacious world i’th’ moon,
19And look to find a constant woman there.

JULIA.

20This is very well, my Lord.

CARDINAL.

This is very well, my Lord. Why do you weep?
21Are tears your justification? The selfsame tears
22Will fall into your husband’s bosom, lady,
23With a loud protestation that you love him
24Above the world. Come, I’ll love you wisely,
25That’s jealously, since I am very certain
26You cannot me make cuckold.

JULIA.

You cannot me make cuckold. I’ll go home
27To my husband.

CARDINAL.

To my husband. You may thank me, lady,
28I have taken you off your melancholy perch,
29Bore you upon my fist, and showed you game,
30And let you fly at it. I pray thee kiss me.
31When thou wast with thy husband, thou wast watched
32Like a tame elephant: (still you are to thank me.)
33Thou hadst only kisses from him, and high feeding,
34But what delight was that? ’Twas just like one
35That hath a little fing’ring on the lute,
36Yet cannot tune it: (still you are to thank me.)

JULIA.

37You told me of a piteous wound i’th’ heart,
38And a sick liver, when you wooed me first,
39And spake like one in physic.

CARDINAL.

And spake like one in physic. Who’s that?

[Enter Servant.]

40Rest firm, for my affection to thee,
41Lightning moves slow to’t.

SERVANT.

Lightning moves slow to’t. Madam, a gentleman
42That’s come post from Malfi, desires to see you.

CARDINAL.

43Let him enter, I’ll withdraw.

Exit.

SERVANT.

Let him enter, I’ll withdraw. He says
44Your husband, old Castruchio, is come to Rome,
45Most pitifully tired with riding post.

[Exit Servant; enter Delio.]

JULIA.

Most pitifully tired with riding post. Signor Delio!
46[aside] ’tis one of my old suitors.aparte

DELIO.

47I was bold to come and see you.

JULIA.

I was bold to come and see you. Sir, you are welcome.

DELIO.

48Do you lie here?

JULIA.

Do you lie here? Sure, your own experience
49Will satisfy you no; our Roman prelates
50Do not keep lodging for ladies.

DELIO.

Do not keep lodging for ladies. Very well.
51I have brought you no commendations from your husband,
52For I know none by him.

JULIA.

For I know none by him. I hear he’s come to Rome?

DELIO.

53I never knew man and beast, of a horse and a knight,
54So weary of each other; if he had had a good back,
55He would have undertook to have borne his horse,
56His breech was so pitifully sore.

JULIA.

His breech was so pitifully sore. Your laughter
57Is my pity.

DELIO.

Is my pity. Lady, I know not whether
58You want money, but I have brought you some.

JULIA.

59From my husband?

DELIO.

From my husband? No, from mine own allowance.

JULIA.

60I must hear the condition, ere I be bound to take it.

DELIO.

61Look on’t, ’tis gold, hath it not a fine colour?

JULIA.

62I have a bird more beautiful.

DELIO.

I have a bird more beautiful. Try the sound on’t.

JULIA.

63A lute string far exceeds it;
64It hath no smell, like cassia or civet,
65Nor is it physical, though some fond doctors
66Persuade us, seethe’t in cullises. I’ll tell you,
67This is a creature bred by—

[Enter Servant.]

SERVANT.

This is a creature bred by— Your husband’s come,
68Hath delivered a letter to the Duke of Calabria,
69That, to my thinking, hath put him out of his wits.

[Exit Servant.]

JULIA.

70Sir, you hear,
71Pray let me know your business and your suit,
72As briefly as can be.

DELIO.

As briefly as can be. With good speed. I would wish you,
73At such time, as you are non-resident
74With your husband, my mistress.

JULIA.

75Sir, I’ll go ask my husband if I shall,
76And straight return your answer.

Exit.

DELIO.

And straight return your answer. Very fine,
77Is this her wit, or honesty that speaks thus?
78I heard one say the Duke was highly moved
79With a letter sent from Malfi. I do fear
80Antonio is betrayed: how fearfully
81Shows his ambition now; unfortunate Fortune!
82They pass through whirlpools, and deep woes do shun,
83Who the event weigh, ere the action’s done.

Exit.

Scene v

[Enter] Cardinal, and Ferdinand, with a letter.

FERDINAND.

1I have this night digged up a mandrake.

CARDINAL.

I have this night digged up a mandrake. Say you?

FERDINAND.

2And I am grown mad with’t.

CARDINAL.

And I am grown mad with’t. What’s the prodigy?

FERDINAND.

3Read there, a sister damned, she’s loose i’th’hilts:
4Grown a notorious strumpet.

CARDINAL.

Grown a notorious strumpet. Speak lower.

FERDINAND.

Grown a notorious strumpet. Speak lower. Lower?
5Rogues do not whisper’t now, but seek to publish’t,
6As servants do the bounty of their lords,
7Aloud; and with a covetous searching eye,
8To mark who note them. Oh confusion seize her,
9She hath had most cunning bawds to serve her turn,
10And more secure conveyances for lust,
11Than towns of garrison, for service.

CARDINAL.

Than towns of garrison, for service. Is’t possible?
12Can this be certain?

FERDINAND.

Can this be certain? Rhubarb, oh for rhubarb
13To purge this choler; here’s the cursed day
14To prompt my memory, and here’t shall stick
15Till of her bleeding heart I make a sponge
16To wipe it out.

CARDINAL.

To wipe it out. Why do you make yourself
17So wild a tempest?

FERDINAND.

So wild a tempest? Would I could be one,
18That I might toss her palace ’bout her ears,
19Root up her goodly forests, blast her meads,
20And lay her general territory as waste,
21As she hath done her honour’s.

CARDINAL.

As she hath done her honour’s. Shall our blood?
22The royal blood of Aragon and Castile,
23Be thus attainted?

FERDINAND.

Be thus attainted? Apply desperate physic,
24We must not now use balsamum, but fire,
25The smarting cupping-glass, for that’s the mean
26To purge infected blood, such blood as hers.
27There is a kind of pity in mine eye,
28I’ll give it to my handkercher; and, now ’tis here,
29I’ll bequeath this to her bastard.

CARDINAL.

I’ll bequeath this to her bastard. What to do?

FERDINAND.

30Why, to make soft lint for his mother’s wounds,
31When I have hewed her to pieces.

CARDINAL.

When I have hewed her to pieces. Cursed creature!
32Unequal Nature, to place women’s hearts
33So far upon the left side.

FERDINAND.

So far upon the left side. Foolish men,
34That e’er will trust their honour in a bark,
35Made of so slight, weak bulrush, as is woman,
36Apt every minute to sink it!

CARDINAL.

37Thus ignorance, when it hath purchased honour,
38It cannot wield it.

FERDINAND.

It cannot wield it. Methinks I see her laughing,
39Excellent hyena! Talk to me somewhat, quickly,
40Or my imagination will carry me
41To see her in the shameful act of sin.

CARDINAL.

42With whom?

FERDINAND.

43Happily, with some strong-thighed bargeman;
44Or one o’th’ wood-yard, that can quoit the sledge
45Or toss the bar, or else some lovely squire
46That carries coals up to her privy lodgings.

CARDINAL.

47You fly beyond your reason.

FERDINAND.

You fly beyond your reason. Go to, mistress!
48’Tis not your whore’s milk, that shall quench my wild-fire
49But your whore’s blood.

CARDINAL.

50How idly shows this rage! which carries you,
51As men conveyed by witches, through the air
52On violent whirlwinds: this intemperate noise
53Fitly resembles deaf men’s shrill discourse,
54Who talk aloud, thinking all other men
55To have their imperfection.

FERDINAND.

To have their imperfection. Have not you
56My palsy?

CARDINAL.

My palsy? Yes, I can be angry
57Without this rupture; there is not in nature
58A thing, that makes man so deformed, so beastly
59As doth intemperate anger; chide yourself:
60You have divers men, who never yet expressed
61Their strong desire of rest but by unrest,
62By vexing of themselves. Come, put yourself
63In tune.

FERDINAND.

In tune. So, I will only study to seem
64The thing I am not. I could kill her now,
65In you, or in myself, for I do think
66It is some sin in us, Heaven doth revenge
67By her.

CARDINAL.

By her. Are you stark mad?

FERDINAND.

By her. Are you stark mad? I would have their bodies
68Burnt in a coal-pit, with the ventage stopped,
69That their cursed smoke might not ascend to Heaven:
70Or dip the sheets they lie in, in pitch or sulphur,
71Wrap them in’t, and then light them like a match:
72Or else to boil their bastard to a cullis,
73And give’t his lecherous father, to renew
74The sin of his back.

CARDINAL.

The sin of his back. I’ll leave you.

FERDINAND.

The sin of his back. I’ll leave you. Nay, I have done;
75I am confident, had I been damned in hell,
76And should have heard of this, it would have put me
77Into a cold sweat. In, in, I’ll go sleep:
78Till I know who leaps my sister, I’ll not stir:
79That known, I’ll find scorpions to string my whips,
80And fix her in a general eclipse.

Exeunt.

Act III

Act III, Scene i

[Enter Antonio and Delio]

ANTONIO.

1Our noble friend, my most beloved Delio,
2Oh, you have been a stranger long at court.
3Came you along with the Lord Ferdinand?

DELIO.

4I did, sir. And how fares your noble Duchess?

ANTONIO.

5Right fortunately well. She’s an excellent
6Feeder of pedigrees: since you last saw her,
7She hath had two children more, a son and daughter.

DELIO.

8Methinks ’twas yesterday. Let me but wink,
9And not behold your face, which to mine eye
10Is somewhat leaner: verily I should dream
11It were within this half hour.

ANTONIO.

12You have not been in law, friend Delio,
13Nor in prison, nor a suitor at the court,
14Nor begged the reversion of some great man’s place,
15Nor troubled with an old wife, which doth make
16Your time so insensibly hasten.

DELIO.

Your time so insensibly hasten. Pray sir tell me,
17Hath not this news arrived yet to the ear
18Of the Lord Cardinal?

ANTONIO.

Of the Lord Cardinal? I fear it hath.
19The Lord Ferdinand, that’s newly come to court,
20Doth bear himself right dangerously.

DELIO.

Doth bear himself right dangerously. Pray, why?

ANTONIO.

21He is so quiet, that he seems to sleep
22The tempest out, as dormice do in winter;
23Those houses, that are haunted, are most still,
24Till the devil be up.

DELIO.

Till the devil be up. What say the common people?

ANTONIO.

25The common rabble do directly say
26She is a strumpet.

DELIO.

She is a strumpet. And your graver heads,
27Which would be politic, what censure they?

ANTONIO.

28They do observe I grow to infinite purchase
29The left-hand way, and all suppose the Duchess
30Would amend it, if she could. For, say they,
31Great princes, though they grudge their officers
32Should have such large and unconfined means
33To get wealth under them, will not complain
34Lest thereby they should make them odious
35Unto the people: for other obligation
36Of love, or marriage, between her and me,
37They never dream of.

[Enter Ferdinand, Duchess and Bosola.]

DELIO.

They never dream of. The Lord Ferdinand
38Is going to bed.

FERDINAND.

Is going to bed. I'll instantly to bed,
39For I am weary: I am to bespeak
40A husband for you.

DUCHESS.

A husband for you. For me, sir! pray who is’t?

FERDINAND.

41The great Count Malateste.

DUCHESS.

The great Count Malateste. Fie upon him,
42A count? He’s a mere stick of sugar-candy,
43You may look quite through him: when I choose
44A husband, I will marry for your honour.

FERDINAND.

45You shall do well in’t. How is’t, worthy Antonio?

DUCHESS.

46But, sir, I am to have private conference with you,
47About a scandalous report is spread
48Touching mine honour.

FERDINAND.

Touching mine honour. Let me be ever deaf to’t:
49One of Pasquil’s paper bullets, court calumny,
50A pestilent air, which princes’ palaces
51Are seldom purged of. Yet, say that it were true,
52I pour it in your bosom, my fixed love
53Would strongly excuse, extenuate, nay deny
54Faults were they apparent in you. Go, be safe
55In your own innocency.

DUCHESS.

In your own innocency. Oh blessed comfort,
56This deadly air is purged.

Exeunt [Dutchess, Antonio, Delio.]

FERDINAND.

This deadly air is purged. Her guilt treads on
57Hot burning cultures. Now Bosola,
58How thrives our intelligence?

BOSOLA.

How thrives our intelligence? Sir, uncertainly:
59’Tis rumored she hath had three bastards, but
60By whom, we may go read i’th’ stars.

FERDINAND.

By whom, we may go read i’th’ stars. Why some
61Hold opinion, all things are written there.

BOSOLA.

62Yes, if we could find spectacles to read them;
63I do suspect, there hath been some sorcery
64Used on the Duchess.

FERDINAND.

Used on the Duchess. Sorcery, to what purpose?

BOSOLA.

65To make her dote on some desertless fellow,
66She shames to acknowledge.

FERDINAND.

She shames to acknowledge. Can your faith give way
67To think there’s power in potions, or in charms,
68To make us love, whether we will or no?

BOSOLA.

69Most certainly.

FERDINAND.

70Away, these are mere gulleries, horrid things
71Invented by some cheating mountebanks
72To abuse us. Do you think that herbs, or charms
73Can force the will? Some trials have been made
74In this foolish practice; but the ingredients
75Were lenitive poisons, such as are of force
76To make the patient mad; and straight the witch
77Swears, by equivocation, they are in love.
78The witchcraft lies in her rank blood: this night
79I will force confession from her. You told me
80You had got, within these two days, a false key
81Into her bed-chamber.

BOSOLA.

Into her bed-chamber. I have.

FERDINAND.

82As I would wish.

BOSOLA.

As I would wish. What do you intend to do?

FERDINAND.

83Can you guess?

BOSOLA.

Can you guess? No.

FERDINAND.

Can you guess? No. Do not ask then.
84He that can compass me, and know my drifts,
85May say he hath put a girdle ’bout the world,
86And sounded all her quick-sands.

BOSOLA.

And sounded all her quick-sands. I do not
87Think so.

FERDINAND.

Think so. What do you think then, pray?

BOSOLA.

Think so. What do you think then, pray? That you
88Are your own chronicle too much: and grossly
89Flatter yourself.

FERDINAND.

Flatter yourself. Give me thy hand; I thank thee.
90I never gave pension but to flatterers,
91Till I entertained thee: farewell,
92That friend a great man’s ruin strongly checks,
93Who rails into his belief all his defects.

Exeunt.

Scene ii

[Enter Duchess, Antonio and Cariola]

DUCHESS.

1Bring me the casket hither, and the glass;
2You get no lodging here to-night, my lord.

ANTONIO.

3Indeed, I must persuade one.

DUCHESS.

Indeed, I must persuade one. Very good:
4I hope in time ’twill grow into a custom,
5That noblemen shall come with cap and knee,
6To purchase a night's lodging of their wives.

ANTONIO.

7I must lie here.

DUCHESS.

I must lie here. Must? you are a Lord of mis-rule.

ANTONIO.

8Indeed, my rule is only in the night.

DUCHESS.

9To what use will you put me?

ANTONIO.

To what use will you put me? We'll sleep together.

DUCHESS.

10Alas, what pleasure can two lovers find in sleep?

CARIOLA.

11My Lord, I lie with her often: and I know
12She’ll much disquiet you.

ANTONIO.

She’ll much disquiet you. See, you are complained of.

CARIOLA.

13For she’s the sprawling’st bedfellow.

ANTONIO.

14I shall like her the better for that.

CARIOLA.

15Sir, shall I ask you a question?

ANTONIO.

16I pray thee Cariola.

CARIOLA.

17Wherefore still, when you lie with my lady
18Do you rise so early?

ANTONIO.

Do you rise so early? Labouring men,
19Count the clock oft’nest Cariola,
20Are glad when their task’s ended.

DUCHESS.

Are glad when their task’s ended. I’ll stop your mouth

[kisses him].

[She kisses him.]

ANTONIO.

21Nay, that’s but one, Venus had two soft doves
22To draw her chariot: I must have another
23[kisses her]. When wilt thou marry, Cariola?

CARIOLA.

[kisses her]. When wilt thou marry, Cariola? Never, my lord.

ANTONIO.

24O fie upon this single life: forgo it.
25We read how Daphne, for her peevish flight
26Became a fruitless bay-tree; Sirinx turned
27To the pale empty reed; Anaxarete
28Was frozen into marble: whereas those
29Which married, or proved kind unto their friends
30Were, by a gracious influence, transhaped
31Into the olive, pomegranate, mulberry:
32Became flowers, precious stones, or eminent stars.

CARIOLA.

33This is a vain poetry: but I pray you tell me,
34If there were proposed me wisdom, riches, and beauty,
35In three several young men, which should I choose?

ANTONIO.

36’Tis a hard question. This was Paris’ case
37And he was blind in’t, and there was great cause:
38For how was’t possible he could judge right,
39Having three amorous goddesses in view,
40And they stark naked? ’Twas a motion
41Were able to benight the apprehension
42Of the severest counsellor of Europe.
43Now I look on both your faces, so well formed
44It puts me in mind of a question, I would ask.

CARIOLA.

45What is’t?

ANTONIO.

What is’t? I do wonder why hard favoured ladies
46For the most part, keep worse-favoured waiting-women,
47To attend them, and cannot endure fair ones.

DUCHESS.

48Oh, that’s soon answered.
49Did you ever in your life know an ill painter
50Desire to have his dwelling next door to the shop
51Of an excellent picture-maker? ’Twould disgrace
52His face-making, and undo him. I prithee
53When were we so merry? My hair tangles.

ANTONIO

54[aside to Cariola]. Pray thee, Cariola, let’s steal forth the room,aparte
55And let her talk to herself: I have divers times
56Served her the like, when she hath chafed extremely.
57I love to see her angry: softly Cariola.

Exeunt [Antonio and Cariola.]

DUCHESS.

58Doth not the colour of my hair ’gin to change?
59When I wax gray, I shall have all the court
60Powder their hair with arras, to be like me:
61You have cause to love me, I ent’red you into my heart.
62[Enter Ferdinand, unseen.] Before you would vouchsafe to call for the keys.
63We shall one day have my brothers take you napping.
64Methinks his presence, being now in court,
65Should make you keep your own bed: but you’ll say
66Love mixed with fear is sweetest. I’ll assure you
67You shall get no more children till my brothers
68Consent to be your gossips. Have you lost your tongue?
69[She sees Ferdinand holding a poniard.] ’Tis welcome:
70For know, whether I am doomed to live, or die,
71I can do both like a prince.

Ferdinand gives her a poniard.

FERDINAND.

I can do both like a prince. Die then, quickly.
72Virtue, where art thou hid? What hideous thing
73Is it, that doth eclipse thee?

DUCHESS.

Is it, that doth eclipse thee? Pray sir hear me―

FERDINAND.

74Or is it true, thou art but a bare name,
75And no essential thing?

DUCHESS.

And no essential thing? Sir—

FERDINAND.

76Do not speak.

DUCHESS.

Do not speak. No, sir:
77I will plant my soul in mine ears, to hear you.

FERDINAND.

78Oh most imperfect light of human reason,
79That mak’st us so unhappy, to foresee
80What we can least prevent. Pursue thy wishes:
81And glory in them: there’s in shame no comfort,
82But to be past all bounds and sense of shame.

DUCHESS.

83I pray sir, hear me: I am married―

FERDINAND.

I pray sir, hear me: I am married― So.

DUCHESS.

84Happily, not to your liking: but for that
85Alas: your shears do come untimely now
86To clip the bird’s wings, that’s already flown.
87Will you see my husband?

FERDINAND.

Will you see my husband? Yes, if I could change
88Eyes with a basilisk.

DUCHESS.

Eyes with a basilisk. Sure, you came hither
89By his confederacy.

FERDINAND.

By his confederacy. The howling of a wolf
90Is music to thee, screech-owl; prithee peace.
91Whate’er thou art, that hast enjoyed my sister,
92(For I am sure thou hear’st me), for thine own sake
93Let me not know thee. I came hither prepared
94To work thy discovery: yet am now persuaded
95It would beget such violent effects
96As would damn us both. I would not for ten millions
97I had beheld thee; therefore use all means
98I never may have knowledge of thy name;
99Enjoy thy lust still, and a wretched life,
100On that condition. And for thee, vild woman,
101If thou do wish thy lecher may grow old
102In thy embracements, I would have thee build
103Such a room for him, as our anchorites
104To holier use inhabit. Let not the sun
105Shine on him, till he’s dead. Let dogs and monkeys
106Only converse with him, and such dumb things
107To whom nature denies use to sound his name.
108Do not keep a paraquito, lest she learn it;
109If thou do love him, cut out thine own tongue
110Lest it bewray him.

DUCHESS.

Lest it bewray him. Why might not I marry?
111I have not gone about, in this, to create
112Any new world, or custom.

FERDINAND.

Any new world, or custom. Thou art undone:
113And thou hast tane that massy sheet of lead
114That hid thy husband’s bones, and folded it
115About my heart.

DUCHESS.

About my heart. Mine bleeds for’t.

FERDINAND.

About my heart. Mine bleeds for’t. Thine? thy heart?
116What should I name’t, unless a hollow bullet
117Filled with unquenchable wild-fire?

DUCHESS.

Filled with unquenchable wild-fire? You are in this
118Too strict: and were you not my princely brother
119I would say too willful. My reputation
120Is safe.

FERDINAND.

121Dost thou know what reputation is?
122I’ll tell thee, to small purpose, since th’instruction
123Comes now too late:
124Upon a time Reputation, Love, and Death
125Would travel o’er the world: and it was concluded
126That they should part, and take three several ways.
127Death told them, they should find him in great battles:
128Or cities plagued with plagues. Love gives them counsel
129To inquire for him ’mongst unambitious shepherds,
130Where dowries were not talked of: and sometimes
131’Mongst quiet kindred, that had nothing left
132By their dead parents. ‘Stay’, quoth Reputation,
133‘Do not forsake me: for it is my nature
134If once I part from any man I meet
135I am never found again.’ And so, for you:
136You have shook hands with Reputation,
137And made him invisible. So fare you well.
138I will never see you more.

DUCHESS.

I will never see you more. Why should only I,
139Of all the other princes of the world
140Be cased up, like a holy relic? I have youth,
141And a little beauty.

FERDINAND.

And a little beauty. So you have some virgins,
142That are witches. I will never see thee more.

Exit.

Enter [Cariola and] Antonio with a pistol.

DUCHESS.

143You saw this apparition?

ANTONIO.

You saw this apparition? Yes: we are
144Betrayed; how came he hither? I should turn
145This, to thee, for that.

[points the pistol at Cariola.]

CARIOLA.

This, to thee, for that. Pray sir do: and when
146That you have cleft my heart, you shall read there,
147Mine innocence.

DUCHESS.

Mine innocence. That gallery gave him entrance.

ANTONIO.

148I would this terrible thing would come again,
149That, standing on my guard, I might relate
150My warrantable love. Ha! what means this?

DUCHESS.

151He left this with me.

She shows the poniard.

ANTONIO.

He left this with me. And it seems, did wish
152You would use it on yourself?

DUCHESS.

You would use it on yourself? His action seemed
153To intend so much.

ANTONIO.

To intend so much. This hath a handle to't,
154As well as a point: turn it towards him, and
155So fasten the keen edge in his rank gall. [knocking]
156How now? Who knocks? More earthquakes?

DUCHESS.

How now? Who knocks? More earthquakes? I stand
157As if a mine, beneath my feet, were ready
158To be blown up.

CARIOLA.

To be blown up. 'Tis Bosola.

DUCHESS.

To be blown up. 'Tis Bosola. Away!
159Oh misery! Methinks unjust actions
160Should wear these masks and curtains; and not we.
161You must instantly part hence: I have fashioned it already.

Ex[it] Ant[onio; enter Bosola.]

BOSOLA.

162The Duke your brother is tane up in a whirlwind;
163Hath took horse, and’s rid post to Rome.

DUCHESS.

Hath took horse, and’s rid post to Rome. So late?

BOSOLA.

164He told me, as he mounted into th’ saddle,
165You were undone.

DUCHESS.

You were undone. Indeed, I am very near it.

BOSOLA.

166What’s the matter?

DUCHESS.

167Antonio, the master of our household
168Hath dealt so falsely with me, in’s accounts:
169My brother stood engaged with me for money
170Tane up of certain Neapolitan Jews,
171And Antonio lets the bonds be forfeit.

BOSOLA.

172Strange:
Strange: [aside] this is cunning.aparte

DUCHESS.

Strange: [aside] this is cunning. And hereupon
173My brother’s bills at Naples are protested
174Against. Call up our officers.

BOSOLA.

Against. Call up our officers. I shall.

Exit.

[Enter Antonio]

DUCHESS.

175The place that you must fly to, is Ancona,
176Hire a house there. I’ll send after you
177My treasure, and my jewels: our weak safety
178Runs upon enginous wheels: short syllables
179Must stand for periods. I must now accuse you
180Of such a feignèd crime, as Tasso calls
181Magnanima mensogna: a noble lie,
182’Cause it must shield our honours: hark, they are coming.

[Enter Bosola and officers.]

ANTONIO.

183Will your Grace hear me?

DUCHESS.

184I have got well by you: you have yielded me
185A million of loss; I am like to inherit
186The people’s curses for your stewardship.
187You had the trick, in audit time to be sick,
188Till I had signed your Quietus; and that cured you
189Without help of a doctor. Gentlemen,
190I would have this man be an example to you all:
191So shall you hold my favour. I pray let him;
192For h’as done that, alas! you would not think of,
193And, because I intend to be rid of him,
194I mean not to publish. Use your fortune elsewhere.

ANTONIO.

195I am strongly armed to brook my overthrow,
196As commonly men bear with a hard year:
197I will not blame the cause on’t; but do think
198The necessity of my malevolent star
199Procures this, not her humour. O the inconstant
200And rotten ground of service, you may see;
201’Tis ev’n like him that, in a winter night,
202Takes a long slumber, o’er a dying fire
203As loath to part from’t: yet parts thence as cold,
204As when he first sat down.

DUCHESS.

As when he first sat down. We do confiscate,
205Towards the satisfying of your accounts,
206All that you have.

ANTONIO.

All that you have. I am all yours; and ’tis very fit
207All mine should be so.

DUCHESS.

All mine should be so. So, sir; you have your pass.

ANTONIO.

208You may see, gentlemen, what ’tis to serve
209A prince with body and soul.

Exit.

BOSOLA.

Here’s an example for extortion; what moisture is
drawn out of the sea, when foul weather comes, pours down,
and runs into the sea again.

DUCHESS.

213I would know what are your opinions
214Of this Antonio.

2 OFFICER.

He could not abide to see a pig’s head gaping,
I thought your Grace would find him a Jew:

3 OFFICER.

I would you had been his officer, for your own sake.

4 OFFICER.

You would have had more money.

1 OFFICER.

He stopped his ears with black wool: and to
those came to him for money said he was thick of hearing.

2 OFFICER.

Some said he was an hermaphrodite, for he
could not abide a woman.

4 OFFICER.

How scurvy proud he would look, when the
treasury was full. Well, let him go.

1 OFFICER.

Yes, and the chippings of the butt’ry fly after
him, to scour his gold chain.

DUCHESS.

227Leave us. What do you think of these?

Exeunt [Officers].

BOSOLA.

228That these are rogues, that in’s prosperity,
229But to have waited on his fortune, could have wished
230His dirty stirrup riveted through their noses:
231And followed after’s mule, like a bear in a ring.
232Would have prostituted their daughters to his lust;
233Made their firstborn intelligencers; thought none happy
234But such as were born under his blessed planet;
235And wore his livery: and do these lice drop off now?
236Well, never look to have the like again;
237He hath left a sort of flatt’ring rogues behind him,
238Their doom must follow. Princes pay flatterers,
239In their own money. Flatterers dissemble their vices,
240And they dissemble their lies, that’s justice.
241Alas, poor gentleman―

DUCHESS.

242Poor! He hath amply filled his coffers.

BOSOLA.

243Sure he was too honest. Pluto the god of riches,
244When he’s sent, by Jupiter, to any man
245He goes limping, to signify that wealth
246That comes on God’s name, comes slowly; but when he’s sent
247On the devil’s errand, he rides post, and comes in by scuttles.
248Let me show you what a most unvalued jewel
249You have, in a wanton humour, thrown away.
250To bless the man shall find him. He was an excellent
251Courtier, and most faithful; a soldier that thought it
252As beastly to know his own value too little,
253As devilish to acknowledge it too much;
254Both his virtue and form deserved a far better fortune:
255His discourse rather delighted to judge itself, than show itself.
256His breast was filled with all perfection,
257And yet it seemed a private whisp’ring room:
258It made so little noise of’t.

DUCHESS.

It made so little noise of’t. But he was basely descended.

BOSOLA.

259Will you make yourself a mercenary herald,
260Rather to examine men’s pedigrees, than virtues?
261You shall want him:
262For know an honest statesman to a prince,
263Is like a cedar, planted by a spring,
264The spring bathes the tree’s root, the grateful tree
265Rewards it with his shadow: you have not done so;
266I would sooner swim to the Bermoothes on
267Two politicians’ rotten bladders, tied
268Together with an intelligencer’s heart string
269Than depend on so changeable a prince’s favour.
270Fare thee well, Antonio, since the malice of the world
271Would needs down with thee, it cannot be said yet
272That any ill happened unto thee,
273Considering thy fall was accompanied with virtue.

DUCHESS.

274Oh, you render me excellent music.

BOSOLA.

Oh, you render me excellent music. Say you?

DUCHESS.

275This good one that you speak of, is my husband.

BOSOLA.

276Do I not dream? Can this ambitious age
277Have so much goodness in’t, as to prefer
278A man merely for worth: without these shadows
279Of wealth, and painted honours? possible?

DUCHESS.

280I have had three children by him.

BOSOLA.

I have had three children by him. Fortunate lady,
281For you have made your private nuptial bed
282The humble and fair seminary of peace.
283No question but many an unbeneficed scholar
284Shall pray for you, for this deed, and rejoice
285That some preferment in the world can yet
286Arise from merit. The virgins of your land,
287That have no dowries, shall hope your example
288Will raise them to rich husbands. Should you want
289Soldiers, ’twould make the very Turks and Moors
290Turn Christians, and serve you for this act.
291Last, the neglected poets of your time,
292In honour of this trophy of a man,
293Raised by that curious engine, your white hand,
294Shall thank you in your grave for’t; and make that
295More reverend than all the cabinets
296Of living princes. For Antonio,
297His fame shall likewise flow from many a pen,
298When heralds shall want coats, to sell to men.

DUCHESS.

299As I taste comfort, in this friendly speech,
300So would I find concealment―

BOSOLA.

So would I find concealment― Oh the secret of my prince,
301Which I will wear on th’inside of my heart.

DUCHESS.

302You shall take charge of all my coin, and jewels,
303And follow him, for he retires himself
304To Ancona.

BOSOLA.

To Ancona. So.

DUCHESS.

To Ancona. So. Whither, within few days,
305I mean to follow thee.

BOSOLA.
